title: What is the difference between map() and flatMap() in streams?
shortTitle: map() vs flatMap(): one-to-one vs one-to-many + flatten
keyPoints: map(Function<T,R>) transforms each element one-to-one: each input T produces exactly one output R.
flatMap(Function<T, Stream<R>>) transforms each element one-to-many and flattens: each T produces a Stream of R, merged into one flat Stream.
If map produces Stream<List<T>> (nested), flatMap produces Stream<T> (flat).
Use flatMap whenever you have nested structures: accounts with transactions, orders with line items, lines with comma-separated values.
flatMap with Optional.stream() (Java 9) extracts present values and removes empty Optionals in one step.
flatMap can produce zero elements (Stream.empty()), one element, or many, making it more flexible than map.
The rule: if you see Stream<List<T>>, Stream<Optional<T>>, or Stream<Stream<T>>, you need flatMap.

s1_definition.oneliner: map transforms one-to-one (wraps), flatMap transforms one-to-many and flattens (unwraps): use flatMap when map gives you Stream<List<T>> but you want Stream<T>.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **map(Function<T,R>)**: transforms each element independently. N elements in, N elements out.
- **flatMap(Function<T, Stream<R>>)**: transforms each element into a Stream and merges all resulting streams into one flat Stream.
- **Signature difference**: map takes `T -> R`, flatMap takes `T -> Stream<R>`.
- **Nesting**: map wraps (produces `Stream<List<R>>`), flatMap unwraps (produces `Stream<R>`).
- **Zero elements**: flatMap can return Stream.empty() for an element, effectively removing it.
- **Optional.stream()**: Java 9 feature; flatMap(Optional::stream) extracts present values and removes empties.
s1_definition.analogy: map is like the currency exchange counter at National Bank of India: each dollar cheque becomes a rupee cheque. One cheque in, one cheque out. flatMap is like splitting a corporate salary cheque into individual employee cheques: one corporate cheque in, 50 individual cheques out, all on the same conveyor belt.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  map (one-to-one, wraps):
  ────────────────────────
  Customer A → [SAV2001, CUR3001]     ← List (wrapped)
  Customer B → [SAV2002]              ← List (wrapped)
  Customer C → [SAV2003, FD4001]      ← List (wrapped)
  Result: Stream<List<String>>  (3 elements, nested)

  flatMap (one-to-many, flattens):
  ────────────────────────────────
  Customer A → SAV2001, CUR3001       ← individual elements
  Customer B → SAV2002                ← individual element
  Customer C → SAV2003, FD4001        ← individual elements
  Result: Stream<String>  (5 elements, flat)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
map transforms one-to-one: each element produces exactly one output. flatMap transforms one-to-many and flattens: each element produces a Stream that is merged into the main Stream. If map gives you Stream<List<T>> (nested), flatMap gives you Stream<T> (flat).

Use flatMap for nested structures (customers with accounts), string splitting (CSV to tokens), Optional extraction (flatMap(Optional::stream)), and merging multiple sources.

Remember one sentence: map wraps each result, flatMap unwraps and flattens, so use flatMap whenever you see nested Stream<List<T>>.
